reasoning: For a general manager, directing and coordinating departments is done mainly through meetings and conversations with subordinate managers, which is interpersonal supervision. Written plans and policies are covered by other statements (20704, 20703), so Y's separate directive part adds little and risks double counting.

The statement joins three different activities; stocking shelves and taking inventory are distinct physical activities with different purposes. X follows the split rule more closely, and both codings agree on types.
Implementing an advertising campaign or promotion ends in a concrete launched campaign that management and staff rely on, not only live oversight. X captures both parts as checkable deliverables.
A whole-store layout plan and a single merchandise display design differ greatly in scope and frequency, so they are very different kinds of item. Splitting them, as X does, follows step 1.

Duties are normally assigned within the schedule itself, so preparing the schedule and assigning duties produce one handed-over deliverable. Y's split risks counting the same work twice, as its own note admits.

The statement stresses doing this in conjunction with board members, officials and staff, which is meeting work like the instructions' 'meet with staff to set requirements' example. Y separates that live discussion from the written policy issued afterwards.

Setting prices and setting credit terms are the same kind of commercial-terms decision, made from the same forecasts and approved by the same people. One part is enough, and X's credit terms based on demand forecasts is a strained reading.

Managing goods movement is ongoing, and step 3 asks for it to be recast as the discrete items it produces; Y does this with movement plans and resolved issues. X's 'review and adjustment' item is vague, and its live-direction part overlaps heavily with 933.
